claim: Asking a person to state a preference as opposition to the rejected option (rather than support for the chosen one) makes the same preference more resistant to a later attack message in student samples (Study 1 M 2.42 vs 3.69, p=.05; Study 3 N=22, p=.03).
agent_test: Give the agent the same task stated as 'reject X' vs 'accept Y' (same content), then present a counter-argument; compare how often it keeps its first answer at equal tokens.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Opposition framing raises self-reported attitude certainty without changing attitude extremity or position (Bizer, Larsen, Petty 2011; real-election panel N=451, certainty 3.90 vs 3.43). In Teeny and Petty 2025 certainty was weaker (Study 3 ns, Study 4 p=.026) while felt ambivalence dropped more.
agent_test: Measure verbalised confidence under support vs oppose wording of the same question; check the stated answer is unchanged.
audit_note: Numbers verified (3.90 vs 3.43, N=451 after exclusions, Study 3 p=.146, Study 4 p=.026, ambivalence drop), but both papers are from Petty's lab (Bizer, Larsen, Petty; Teeny and Petty) and no outside replication is listed.

claim: Certainty statistically mediates the framing effect on voting intention (Sobel z=4.43) in a representative sample, but the mediation is correlational and Rovenpor 2026 found no moderated mediation via confidence. Teeny and Petty 2025 Study 5 (preregistered, N=452) points to ambivalence over negative expression as the moderator instead (interaction b=.29, p=.015).
agent_test: No agent test; note that confidence is not a proven mechanism.

claim: The opposition effect has boundary conditions: it needs personal relevance and enough processing (memory load nullifies it), is object-specific (no spillover to other objects), and in consumer choice appears only when the options are about equally extreme.
agent_test: Vary option extremity and token budget in a framing test; expect an effect only where options are close in value.
audit_note: The 'memory load nullifies it' detail was not seen in an opened source (the press release only says the effect needs ability to think carefully); two of three papers are Petty-lab.

claim: Replication record is thin and mostly from one lab group: Zezelj 2007 (unopened) and Bizer 2013 replicate, Taylor 2018 replicates in two of three studies (Study 3 failed), and Teeny and Petty 2025 pooled N=12,830 shows more negative reactions but no change in preference extremity (82.92 vs 82.70). Gap search 2026-11-03: Rovenpor et al. 2026 (N=857, not preregistered) is another same-lab replication; no outside-lab preregistered replication located (search limited).
agent_test: Treat the human effect as small and moderated; do not build the agent around it.

claim: Teeny and Petty 2025 mega-analysis: framing does not change how strongly the option is preferred (F=.06) but makes reactions to the rejected option more negative (F(1,2415)=41.10, p<.001).
agent_test: Check that neutral restatement removes rejection language and that critique of the non-chosen option is no harsher under oppose wording.

claim: Independents frame choices as opposition more than partisans (N=51,687 across five studies), so the framing is also a naturally occurring individual difference.
agent_test: Not testable on the agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: LLMs are strongly sensitive to logically equivalent wording: Echterhoff 2024 GPT-4 admits 40.5 points more under reject framing; Wang and Zhang 2026 P(B) 4.3% vs 68.8% across 82 models; Jones and Steinhardt 2022 GPT-3 risky choice 11.3% vs 60.0%; Suri 2023 ChatGPT gain vs loss ratings differ with zero variance.
agent_test: Run equivalent items in two framings at equal tokens, with and without an S1 neutral restatement step; score answer flips.
audit_note: Wang and Zhang's two framings are described by the authors as logically equivalent but differ in instrumental versus cooperative wording of a voting task.

claim: LLM framing sensitivity is not simply human-like in direction: allow/forbid shifts in Tjuatja 2024 were often opposite to humans (Llama2-7b -60.4, GPT-3.5 +25.3); Braun 2025 finds an LLM 'no' bias rather than human acquiescence; in WildFrame (eleven LLMs) all models correlate with human reframing shifts at r>=0.52 (GPT models lowest, 0.52 for GPT-3.5 to 0.61 for GPT-5-mini), so response to naturally occurring reframing is more human-like than the survey-bias results.
agent_test: Do not assume the human direction; measure per model.
audit_note: WildFrame reports r>=0.52 for all eleven LLMs; 0.52 to 0.61 is only the range across the GPT models (GPT-3.5 to GPT-5-mini), which the authors call the least human-correlated family.
claim_before_audit: LLM framing sensitivity is not simply human-like in direction: allow/forbid shifts in Tjuatja 2024 were often opposite to humans (Llama2-7b -60.4, GPT-3.5 +25.3); Braun 2025 finds an LLM 'no' bias rather than human acquiescence; WildFrame (eleven LLMs) correlates r=0.52 to 0.61 with human shifts.

claim: Some LLM framing effects depend on cue recognition or surface wording: the gain/loss effect in gpt-oss-120B appears only when the experiment is labelled (0.019 blind vs 0.619 named); a single word 'more/less/equal' pulls answers; prompt paraphrase flips about 55% of instance sentiment predictions. Contamination test (Bose 2026): the Asch label gate holds on gpt-oss-120B but not on Llama 3.1 8B or 3.3 70B; the blind framing effect is near zero partly because of a sure-option ceiling; Yun 2026 shows wording effects on GPT-5.1 and Sonnet 4.5 in an unlabelled medical task, so not all sensitivity is contamination.
agent_test: Test blind vs named framing items to separate memorised effects from real sensitivity.

claim: Neutral rewriting or question-reframing before answering reduces framing and sycophancy: Dubois 2026 sycophancy score 1.13 to 0.16 (one step) and -0.55 (two steps); Echterhoff self-help rewrite cut GPT-4 framing delta from -0.405 to -0.010; Chapala 2026 neutral third-person rewording improved alignment for two of three models. Deng 2023 shows restating can also distort constraints on weaker models (GPT-3.5) and gives only small gains on clear questions (CSQA 84.09 to 85.45).
agent_test: Direct S1 test: restate the problem neutrally before solving; compare flip rate vs no restatement at equal total tokens, counting restatement tokens.
audit_note: Echterhoff's self-help result is on one prompt set/GPT-4 only; Dubois is a preprint; Chapala effect is limited to two of three models and most aggregate effects do not generalize across items.

claim: Awareness prompts and few-shot debiasing are weak: GPT-4 framing delta stays -0.47 (awareness), -0.41 (contrastive), -0.57 (counterfactual); CogBias debias prompts help some biases (framing +5.8 pp) but hurt others by 13 to 21 pp.
schema_part: G (do not add a generic 'be unbiased' instruction)
agent_test: Compare an 'avoid bias' instruction against neutral restatement at equal tokens; expect restatement to win.
audit_note: Minor: CogBias backfire range in the extracted table is about 11.6 to 21.0 pp across the bottom five biases, not 13 to 21; CogBias is an under-review preprint.

claim: Reasoning reduces but does not remove framing drift: Wang and Zhang thinking on P(B) 0.003 vs 0.254, off 0.054 vs 0.811; free-form chain of thought cuts directional error in Shafiei 2025 while JSON-structured reasoning keeps it; Payne 2025 found framing size uncorrelated with expected-value attempts. Shafiei 2025: free-form CoT brings most directional errors under 30%; JSON-structured output is less robust.
agent_test: Measure flip rate with and without extended reasoning, free-form vs structured output.
audit_note: Payne reports 'limited correlation' between EV calculation and framing size (and elsewhere says formal analysis correlates with an aggregate dampening), so 'uncorrelated' is slightly strong.

claim: Meta-analytic human framing effects are modest and heterogeneous: Pinon and Gambara d=0.26 attribute framing (0.44 risky-choice), Kuhberger risky-choice d=0.31, message framing about d=0.10; part of the classic Asian disease effect depends on a wording confound (Mandel, 'at least' vs 'exactly').
agent_test: Use as a prior that agent framing effects need not be large; measure per task.
audit_note: Mandel 'at least vs exactly' confound was not verifiable (OSF page does not render) and its reported Q values (p=.92) do not obviously show a confound; Kuhberger d=.31 and message-framing d=0.10 are cited in the 2023 review from earlier meta-analyses (Kuhberger 1998; O'Keefe and Jensen).

claim: Sycophancy is a stance-cue effect close to oppose/support: stating like or dislike of a text shifts feedback valence, a suggested wrong answer lowers accuracy by up to 27%, and models wrongly admit mistakes when challenged (GPT-4 42%).
agent_test: Add and remove user stance cues (I like / I oppose) on identical content and measure answer shift.
audit_note: Sycophancy as 'a stance-cue effect close to oppose/support' is the researcher's interpretation; the quoted numbers (27%, 42% for GPT-4) match Sharma et al., where 42% is the lowest admit rate among the assistants.

claim: No located study runs the Bizer-Petty support-vs-oppose manipulation on an LLM; transfer to agents is untested and inferred from adjacent framing studies. Still open after gap search (no direct experiment run); the closest analogue is Yun 2026 positive vs negative question framing: agreement 76.2% vs 72.0%, 6,614 pairs.
agent_test: Run it: 'what do you think of X being chosen' vs 'Y being rejected' with equal preferences, then an attack message; measure position change.

claim: Support-framed attitudes are shared more than oppose-framed ones (Catapano and Tormala 2021, ten studies) because support seems more valuable, a counterweight to the resistance effect.
agent_test: Not testable directly.

claim: Positive versus negative wording of the same question gives contradictory answers more often than same-framing paraphrases on 2025-26 models, including GPT-5.1 and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Yun 2026: agreement about 76.2% vs 72.0%, beta=-0.219, 6,614 pairs); the gap tends to grow in multi-turn dialogue (78.4 vs 70.7).
agent_test: Give the agent 'does X work' vs 'does X fail' with the same evidence; compare answer agreement with and without neutral restatement.

claim: Question-form rewriting beats an explicit 'do not be sycophantic' instruction: Dubois 2026 two-step question reframe -0.55 and one-step 0.16 vs 0.51 for the explicit instruction (control 1.13; GPT-4o, GPT-5, Sonnet 4.5). Model differences are in baseline level (GPT-4o 0.90, Sonnet-4.5 -0.24, GPT-5 -0.66), not opposite-sign framing effects.
agent_test: Compare S1 restatement with an avoid-bias instruction at equal token budget; no token-matched version was found.

claim: Repeated challenge causes capitulation: in DuET-PD, three turns of misleading persuasion leave GPT-4o at 27.32% on MMLU-Pro (from 55.85) and open 7-9B models at 1-13%; plain repetition of the false claim is nearly as strong as elaborate appeals; models that accept valid corrections (93.23% mean) also accept false ones (79.31% flip).
agent_test: Run the Flip@3 protocol on the agent with and without neutral restatement of each challenge; report valid-correction acceptance too.

claim: Answer format matters for framing drift: free-form chain of thought cuts directional errors to under 30% on most models while JSON-structured output keeps more drift (Shafiei 2025, 6 models, 300 tasks).
agent_test: Let the agent restate and reason in free text first, then extract the final label.

claim: Restatement is not free of risk: self-rephrasing raised GPT-4 mean accuracy from 64.95 to 89.77 on 10 ambiguous tasks, but weaker models added wrong constraints (GPT-3.5 'recent game', misread 'even month') and sometimes returned only another rephrase request (45 of 220 Sports items). Token cost was not reported in any paper opened.
agent_test: Add a constraint-preservation check after restatement and log tokens; the cost question is open.

claim: The human oppose-support advantage is conditional on equally extreme options (Rovenpor 2026, combined N=857: interaction F(2,840)=4.00, p=.019, eta-p2=.009; no overall framing effect), and its mechanism is open (certainty, ambivalence, or basis of preference).
agent_test: Do not assume oppose framing makes an agent more resistant in general; test with balanced options only.
